title: Understanding Utility Bills
objectives: Read and interpret a utility bill including charges, due dates, and account numbers
Set up electricity, gas, water, and internet services in a new home
Identify when a bill may contain an error and know how to dispute it
Use gerunds and infinitives correctly when describing household habits and actions

reading_passage.title: Making Sense of Your Monthly Bills
reading_passage.text:
When Abdullahi moved into his first apartment in Portland, he was surprised to receive five separate bills in his first month: electricity, gas, water, internet, and renter's insurance. In Somalia, he had never managed utility accounts independently, and the bills were confusing at first — full of account numbers, service periods, usage graphs, and small print about late fees.

His case worker at IRCO helped him understand the basics. Every bill shows the billing period — the dates the service covers — and the due date, which is the last day to pay without a late fee. Most utility companies in Oregon offer a budget billing option, which averages your expected yearly costs into equal monthly payments so that your bill stays predictable, even in winter when heating costs rise.

Abdullahi learned to check three things on every bill: the meter reading to confirm that usage was calculated correctly, the total amount due, and the due date. When his electricity bill one month seemed unusually high — nearly double the previous month — he called Portland General Electric and was told his meter had been estimated rather than read. After a technician came to read the actual meter, the bill was corrected.

Setting up utilities requires contacting each company separately. Most accept applications online or by phone. You will need to provide your address, a move-in date, and sometimes a deposit if you have no credit history. Many companies offer low-income assistance programmes — Portland General Electric's OHAP programme, for example, can reduce monthly bills for qualifying families.
reading_passage.source: Adapted from newcomer financial literacy materials produced by Immigrant and Refugee Community Organisation (IRCO), Portland, Oregon, 2023

glossary.meaning: a basic service such as electricity, gas, water, or internet that is provided to a home
the span of dates that a bill covers, showing how much of the service was used during that time
a payment option that spreads annual costs into equal monthly amounts to make bills easier to predict
a measurement of how much electricity, gas, or water a home has used, taken from a device on the property
an upfront payment required by some companies as security, often returned after a period of on-time payments

comprehension.question: What three things did Abdullahi learn to check on every utility bill?
comprehension.answer: The meter reading, the total amount due, and the due date.

comprehension.question: What does the author imply when they say the bills were 'full of small print about late fees'?
comprehension.answer: The author implies that utility bills contain important but easy-to-overlook information about penalties for late payment — and that newcomers need to read carefully to avoid unexpected charges.

comprehension.question: What does 'budget billing' mean in the second paragraph?
comprehension.answer: A payment option that averages your expected yearly costs into equal monthly payments — so your bill stays consistent and does not spike in winter when heating costs are higher.

comprehension.question: Why did Abdullahi's electricity bill suddenly double one month?
comprehension.answer: Because his meter had been estimated rather than actually read — the company guessed his usage instead of measuring it precisely, which produced an inaccurate and inflated bill.

language_focus.title: Gerunds and Infinitives After Common Verbs
language_focus.explanation: Many English verbs are followed by either a gerund (verb + -ing) or an infinitive (to + verb). Some verbs always take a gerund: avoid, enjoy, consider, finish, suggest. Some always take an infinitive: need, want, decide, agree, plan, refuse. Knowing which pattern a verb follows makes your English sound natural and accurate.

examples.sentence: I need to contact the utility company before the due date.
examples.note: 'Need' is always followed by an infinitive — 'need to contact,' not 'need contacting.'

examples.sentence: I avoid leaving lights on in empty rooms to reduce my electricity bill.
examples.note: 'Avoid' is always followed by a gerund — 'avoid leaving,' not 'avoid to leave.'

practice.sentence: Choose the correct form: 'She finished ___ (set up / setting up) the internet account yesterday.'
practice.answer: She finished setting up the internet account yesterday. ('Finish' is followed by a gerund.)

practice.sentence: Choose the correct form: 'He decided ___ (switch / to switch) to budget billing after his high winter bill.'
practice.answer: He decided to switch to budget billing after his high winter bill. ('Decide' is followed by an infinitive.)

practice.sentence: Which is correct? A) I enjoy to read my bills carefully. B) I enjoy reading my bills carefully.
practice.answer: B) 'Enjoy' is always followed by a gerund — 'enjoy reading,' not 'enjoy to read.'

vocabulary_in_context.definition: A basic service — such as electricity, gas, water, or internet — supplied to a home or building
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: He was surprised to receive five separate bills in his first month: electricity, gas, water, internet, and renter's insurance.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: The range of dates that a bill covers, recording what service was used during that time
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: Every bill shows the billing period — the dates the service covers — and the due date.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: An upfront payment held by a company as security, often returned after a record of on-time payments
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: You will need to provide your address, a move-in date, and sometimes a deposit if you have no credit history.

speaking_task.context: You have just received your electricity bill and the total is nearly three times higher than last month. You believe there may be an error. You are calling Portland General Electric's customer service line.
speaking_task.prompt: Call the utility company and explain the problem clearly. Give your account details, describe the issue, explain why you think there is an error, and ask what steps will be taken to investigate. Use at least one gerund and one infinitive in your response.
useful_language: I'm calling about my electricity bill for the billing period ending March 1st — the amount doesn't seem correct.
I've been trying to reduce my usage this month, not increase it.
I'd like to request a meter inspection to confirm the reading is accurate.
speaking_task.model_answer: Good morning. I'm calling about my electricity bill for the billing period ending March 1st. My account number is 4471-B. The bill shows a charge of $280, but my bill is usually around $90. I've been trying to reduce my energy use this month — I started turning off appliances when I'm not using them. I'd like to request a meter inspection to confirm the reading is accurate. Can you tell me what I need to do to dispute this charge, and how long the process will take?

writing_workshop.model_text:
Dear Portland General Electric,

I am writing to dispute a charge on my most recent electricity bill, account number 5832-A, for the billing period January 15th to February 15th. The bill shows a total of $312.00, which is significantly higher than my usual monthly charge of approximately $95.00.

I believe the bill may be based on an estimated meter reading rather than an actual reading. I request that a technician visit my home to take an accurate meter reading at your earliest convenience.

Please confirm receipt of this letter and advise on the next steps to resolve this matter.

Sincerely,
Abdullahi Hassan
writing_workshop.model_analysis: Notice how the letter includes specific account details, the billing period, the disputed amount, and a clear reason for the dispute. The writer remains professional and uses infinitives ('I request that a technician visit,' 'to resolve this matter') and a gerund ('billing period') naturally.
writing_workshop.task: Write a short letter or email to a utility company about a problem with your bill. Include your account information, the billing period, the issue you have identified, and a clear request for action. Use at least one gerund and one infinitive structure.
success_criteria: Include account or reference details and the billing period in the first paragraph
Clearly state what the problem is and why you believe there is an error
Use at least one gerund (e.g., 'billing period,' 'setting up') and one infinitive (e.g., 'I need to dispute,' 'to confirm the reading')

quiz.question: What is 'budget billing,' according to the passage?
options: A discount programme for low-income families
A payment option that divides annual costs into equal monthly amounts
A plan that allows you to pay your bill late without a penalty
A service that estimates usage based on similar households nearby
quiz.explanation: The passage defines budget billing as a way to 'average your expected yearly costs into equal monthly payments so that your bill stays predictable, even in winter when heating costs rise.'

quiz.question: Why was Abdullahi's electricity bill nearly double one month?
options: He had left the heating on all month by mistake
The utility company had raised its prices
His meter had been estimated rather than actually read
He had moved into a larger apartment
quiz.explanation: The passage explains: 'he was told his meter had been estimated rather than read. After a technician came to read the actual meter, the bill was corrected.'

quiz.question: Which sentence uses a gerund correctly?
options: She avoided to leave the heating on overnight.
She avoided leaving the heating on overnight.
She avoided leave the heating on overnight.
She avoided to leaving the heating on overnight.
quiz.explanation: 'Avoid' must be followed by a gerund (verb + -ing) — 'avoided leaving' is the correct form.

quiz.question: According to the passage, what may a utility company require from someone with no credit history?
options: A letter of recommendation from a community organisation
A co-signer who guarantees the account
Proof of employment and monthly income
quiz.explanation: The passage states: 'You will need to provide your address, a move-in date, and sometimes a deposit if you have no credit history.'
